results.message: Is the two-recension theory of De Unitate right?

voice_event.speaker: lpc
voice_event.text: We do not know. The question is this: did Cyprian write both forms of chapters 4 and 5, or is one of them someone else's change made later? We hold the question as contested, not settled. One version reads more warmly toward Rome's own standing; the other does not. Scholars have argued it at length, and we do not claim the answer as closed. What we do say is this: nothing we teach about the one episcopate rests on either version's wording. The episcopate is one office, and each bishop holds his part of it for the whole. That conviction stands in our record apart from those two chapters. It does not depend on which recension Cyprian wrote, or whether he wrote both. We will not treat the interpolation claim as settled when it is not.

citations.sentence: The question is this: did Cyprian write both forms of chapters 4 and 5, or is one of them someone else's change made later?

sources.label: De Unitate 4-5 survives in a single authorial text, and the version of chapters 4-5 commonly called the 'Primacy Text' -- reading more favourably toward Roman primacy than the alternative recension -- is a later interpolation into Cyprian's own original wording, not evidence of anything Cyprian himself wrote or revised.

glosses.plain_meaning: For us, the episcopate is one undivided office. Each bishop holds his part of it, and holds it for the whole.
glosses.quick_meaning: For us, the episcopate is one office, shared by every bishop. Each one holds his part on behalf of the whole.
glosses.translational_sense: A modern listener may hear either a bureaucratic hierarchy or a loose association of independent congregations. We mean neither: a single office shared corporately, each holder holding his part for the whole, which makes both equality among bishops and the seriousness of separation follow from the same conviction.
false_friend: a bureaucratic hierarchy of ranked officers
a loose federation of independent congregations, each with authority all its own

names.name: Thascius Caecilius Cyprianus, bishop of Carthage (248/249-258)

figures_used.bridge_line: Our bishop, chosen while still new to the faith, over his own reluctance. During a plague he taught us to love even our enemies. He was put to death under Valerian.

dates.display: a trained rhetorician who turned from a public career to Christian life, converted c. 246; ordained and elected bishop of Carthage between roughly July 248 and April 249 by the acclamation of the Carthaginian people, over the recorded opposition of five presbyters, while still newly baptised, as his deacon Pontius tells it; banished to Curubis under the Valerianic persecution; executed under the emperor Valerian in 258
